rationale: The judgment changed, so a complete assessment is returned. Since the incumbent, the ledger has admitted seven primary or near-primary texts — Schmidt's 2006 note and the excavation team's 2016 discussion of Pillar 43, the abstract of Vidale and Micheli's wear study, the abstract of Pitts and colleagues' study of Hoa Hakananai'a, Verbrugghe and Wickersham's Berossus, the team's Urfa Man post, and one page of Wiggermann via a blog transcription — so the incumbent's premise that every evidence record came from the founder's page no longer holds and its 'how thin the ground is' section is replaced by a statement of what the two kinds of source now decide. Per-claim verdicts move: DEEP-C012 from unresolved to well_supported on DEEP-E028 (the team's own 'no final decision'); DEEP-C009 to provisionally_supported on DEEP-E035 with DEEP-E038 as the authors' own limit; DEEP-C059 to provisionally_supported on DEEP-E068 and DEEP-E069 (statue, then komari, then reliefs); DEEP-C044 to weakly_supported on DEEP-E055 (water half only, transcription unchecked); DEEP-C053 to weakly_supported on the disclosed sibling basis of DEEP-E043 (C081) and DEEP-E079 (C086), the iconographic half still anchor-only. DEEP-C072 is added to the featured set: it is the excavators' stated position on the contact account's central rung — intermediates — and is now evidenced (DEEP-E061, DEEP-E062); the load-bearing set takes it in. Weakest links drop C009 and C059, which now have records, and take C028 and C053, whose grading rests on thin or indirect footing. The case verdict remains unresolved but for a changed reason: not for want of any primary text, but because the primaries confirm what the objects are and when their carvings were made without producing a dated intermediate or a composite count, while the only positive signal (DEEP-E020) is untested against retelling; the record whose removal would most change the verdict is still DEEP-E020. Anchor-only observational claims (C015, C028, C031, C054, C037) stay unresolved at low confidence; methodological anchor-only claims are graded on priors stated as priors, with sibling records named where they bear. Research: DEEP-R001 is marked answered — the Pillar 43 discussion and the Vidale abstract were retrieved and their records now decide C009 and C012 at the level read; the remaining team texts are DEEP-R005's target and the unread Vidale body is a blocked source. The crux order leads with the blind human lineup, then the excavators' named intermediate (R004), the navel source histories (R002) and the full run of team statements on Pillar 43 (R005). The article now tells the Rapa Nui, Pillar 43, banduddû, Jiroft, Oannes and Urfa Man passages in the primaries' words, marks each anchor-only caption as such, and reports Pitts and colleagues' reading of the reliefs against a nineteenth-century recorded myth as the clearest illustration in the ledger of what the retelling account predicts; incumbent prose on the catalogue, navel, serpent, flood and method themes is trimmed to make room, so length stays near the incumbent's. Question and accounts are unchanged; the article groups the accounts exactly as the field does, with the lost-civilisation account told as the strongest variant of the common-source account. No panel dissent is in the packet.
article:
## The pattern people see

Set the pictures out in a row and the resemblance does its work before anyone has made an argument. An eagle-headed figure strides across a palace wall from Nimrud with a bucket in one hand and a cone in the other. A vulture spreads its wings on a Neolithic pillar at Göbekli Tepe, and along the pillar's top edge sit three arched shapes with handles. A seated man on an Olmec boulder from La Venta holds a small bag inside the coils of a crested serpent. Two bird-headed men face one another on the back of a statue taken from Rapa Nui. A netted stone at Delphi marks the navel of the world; so, in their own languages, do places in the Andes and the Pacific. A teacher comes from the sea, brings the arts, and leaves. A flood drowns everyone but a few.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P01}

The eye reads these as kin. The question is whether history does — and how one could tell. The founder's Deep Memory pages ask it without answering it, and their working rule is the one this case adopts: [the historical meaning of a visual resemblance depends on the objects' dates, contexts, differences and possible connections, not on the resemblance alone]{claim=DEEP-C002}. What follows applies that rule, object by object, to what the ledger holds.

### Two kinds of source

The ledger draws on two kinds of text. The first is the founder's home page — a self-published, AI-assisted essay that reports five investigations its author ran. It supplies the catalogue frequencies, the lineup result and the image and text pilots. The method calls these *self-reports*: an author's statement of an unaudited result, with data and code not in hand, admitted as weak support at most. The second kind is the primary literature behind particular objects: the excavator's first published note on Pillar 43 and his team's later discussion of it; the abstract of the wear-trace study of the Jiroft object; the abstract of the published study of Hoa Hakananai'a; the translated fragments of Berossus; the excavation team's post on Urfa Man; and one page of Wiggermann's edition of the Assyrian ritual texts, seen through a blog's transcription. These settle several questions about what the objects are and when they were carved. None of them tests the thesis itself, and several claims that matter — the four navel names, the Viracocha label, the flood coding, the AI judges' disagreement — still stand on the page alone, with no record for or against. Where that is so, this article says so.

## Four accounts, set side by side

The founding pages name four explanations and insist that more than one can be true in different cases. This edition treats them as the live accounts.

- **A common source.** The forms and stories descend from one ancestor and were carried outward. In its strongest version — the lost-civilisation account — that ancestor is an unknown society of great age and capability whose emissaries taught the rest. It predicts that specific composites (this pose with this object in this arrangement; this arrival, teaching and departure in this order) recur across the compared cultures more often than chance, and that the oldest examples cluster near the source.
- **Long-distance contact.** Particular cultures met and exchanged images or stories, with no single ancestor. It predicts dated intermediates, a plausible route, and resemblance strongest where the route runs.
- **Independent invention, or convergence.** Similar bodies, animals, materials and practical problems make similar forms; similar disasters make similar stories. It predicts that the broad classes are common everywhere, that a handle or a folded hand appears wherever carvers face the same problem, and that specific composites do not travel together more than comparison bundles do.
- **Later retelling.** Much of the resemblance is made after the fact: by translation, by borrowing after contact, by comparative writers who smooth different stories into one biography, and by selecting matching examples from a very large pool. It predicts that similarity grows between an original account and its modern summary, and that details of a famous version turn up unevenly, where that version was preached.

The themes follow in turn: what the ledger holds for each account, and what observation would decide between them.

## Bird-men

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P10}

The gallery runs from the shaft scene at Lascaux — a stick-figure man with a bird's head falling beside a wounded bison, a bird on a staff nearby — through Egyptian gods and Assyrian genii to costumed dancers in the Americas and the birdman cult of Rapa Nui. The founding pages supply the first objection themselves: [the description “bird-man” groups at least three distinct ideas — a deity with a bird's head, a person wearing feathers, and a person transforming into a bird]{claim=DEEP-C004}. If the compared images fall into different ones of these, the parallel is not one resemblance but three weaker ones. The distinction is graded here on the prior that these are different concepts; no evidence record has yet sorted the gallery into them.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P05}

The Rapa Nui example is where dates bite, and it is the one bird-man in the ledger with a published study behind it. Hoa Hakananai'a, the basalt moai taken from Orongo to London in 1868, carries low reliefs on its back. The study's abstract gives their order: the statue was made with a tapering base to stand in the ground; two *komari* — stylised female genitalia — were subsequently added; and succeeding those came the bas-relief carvings. So [the birdman carvings were added later than the statue's manufacture]{claim=DEEP-C059}: they are a later use of an older monument, not part of its design. The authors [read the reliefs as a single composition narrating the island's birdman myth as it was recorded in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries]{claim=DEEP-C080}, a reading they say is supported by photographs taken in Chile in 1868. The comparison text for these birdmen, in other words, is an ethnohistoric one written down after European contact; the study reads them against no prehistoric source. The founder's page dates the statue to about 1000–1200 CE and lists a sooty tern between the birdmen's beaks, paddles, a ring and a girdle; the abstract [gives no absolute date]{claim=DEEP-C058} and does not itemise those motifs, so both are held here on the page's word until the body of the paper or the museum record is read. Whatever the date, the Rapa Nui leg of the comparison stands an ocean from Lascaux and Nimrud and many millennia later than either.

The catalogue experiment gives the other half. The page reports that [a broad bird-person motif class occurs in 55% of 926 sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C005}. A *base rate* is how often a thing occurs in the population at large; a motif found in more than half of all sampled traditions is one you would expect to meet in any two cultures picked at random. That figure, if it holds, is the strongest reason in the ledger not to be surprised by a bird-man in two places. But the page qualifies its own number twice, and the ledger records both: the catalogue's coverage is uneven, particularly for the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui — the very regions compared — and broad narrative categories are not the specific images or place names in the claim. A class that includes every winged soul and feathered dancer does not say how often a profile head, a bent limb and a rounded form nearby occur together. That composite, not the class, is what a common-source account needs, and no one has counted it.

## The handled objects

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P02}

Four objects make the comparison: the three arched forms on Pillar 43, the bucket carried by the Assyrian genii, the carved chlorite objects from the Halil Rud valley in Iran, and the small pouch held by the seated figure on Monument 19 at La Venta. Their outlines rhyme. Then the pages make the distinction the theme turns on: [shape and function are separate questions]{claim=DEEP-C065} — and the primaries now in the ledger show how differently the four stand on the second.

At Göbekli Tepe the shape is the excavator's own description. Klaus Schmidt's first published note on the pillar records, above the vulture, [three big, similarly carved box-like objects with handle-like attachments]{claim=DEEP-C067}, [each accompanied by an animal]{claim=DEEP-C068}. He names no function. Ten years later his team's discussion of the pillar weighs a reading of the three forms as the enclosures themselves seen from the side, and closes by saying that a final decision on the meaning of these images is not possible at the moment. [The function of the three handled forms is uncertain]{claim=DEEP-C012}, in the words of the people who dug them up — the best-supported statement in this theme, and one a later team publication could sharpen in either direction.

For the Assyrian object the ledger holds the textual identification, at one remove. Wiggermann's edition of the protective-spirit rituals, seen through a blog's transcription of a single page, states that [*banduddû* unquestionably denotes the bucket held by many figures of the reliefs]{claim=DEEP-C043}, and that in rituals it was filled with water: the exorcist is told to take the bucket, bring water from the mouth of the twin rivers, cast a holy spell over it and sprinkle it over the man. That is the water half of [the bucket-and-purifier interpretation]{claim=DEEP-C044}; the cone in the genie's other hand is not in the transcribed text, and the transcription has not been checked against the printed page. Weakly supported, then, but supported: the Nimrud object is a known ritual vessel.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P04}

The Jiroft object is the one case where function has been tested physically. The abstract of Vidale and Micheli's study describes a chlorite “hand-bag” in the museum in Tehran examined for the wear traces clearly visible on its handle and along its contour, and reads that strong wear as showing that [the object hung for a long time on a cord]{claim=DEEP-C009} — gradually polished, they suggest, by rubbing against a soft, cloth-covered surface. The founder's caption is a faithful summary of their reading. The authors add the limit themselves: the inference rests on a single object and is far from being granted. So one Halil Rud object was probably a hung container; the class is not thereby settled, and whether this is the very object photographed above is not confirmed from the abstract.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P03}

At La Venta the ledger holds only the page's captions: the figure's pouch is [usually read as an incense bag]{claim=DEEP-C010}, and the serpent framing him is [called the earliest known feathered serpent]{claim=DEEP-C003}. Neither has an evidence record.

Set the four out again and the comparison is now legible: a known Assyrian ritual bucket, one Iranian object that hung on a cord, a Mesoamerican pouch read as a bag on the page's word, and three Anatolian forms whose own excavators decline to say what they are. The outlines rhyme; the functions run from established to unknown. What a common-source account needs, and convergence does not predict, is that the *particular* handle — its attachment, its proportion to the body, its decoration, the figures beside it — recurs across the compared objects more often than across a control set of handled containers from cultures known to be unconnected. No one has run that comparison.

The excavators have also been asked the contact question directly. To a reader who raised later Sumerian and Assyrian bird figures in a similar posture, a team member replied that some of the site's imagery may survive into later seal images, but that at the moment [there are far too many missing links to be sure about the extent of any survival of Early Neolithic imagery, or the changes in meaning it may have undergone]{claim=DEEP-C072}. That is the contact account's requirement — dated intermediates and a route — stated as unmet by the people best placed to know, with one candidate class of intermediates named. The research item that tests it stands second on this edition's agenda.

## Pigs, lizards and other stone animals

A low body, a raised back and a projecting snout make a boar legible across any distance; splayed limbs and open jaws make a crouching predator. The page reports that the excavation team's discussion of Enclosure C [distinguishes boars from snarling predators]{claim=DEEP-C045}, reading the animals in their arrangement rather than as isolated silhouettes; the claim is held on its anchor, with no evidence record yet. The founding pages are right that “lizard” should stay a proposed identification where the animal is uncertain, and that the useful next comparison is with other securely identified pig and boar sculptures rather than with whatever looks alike. Nothing in this theme is graded; it awaits objects with museum numbers.

## The navel of the world

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P06}

The linguistic parallel is the most evocative and, on inspection, the most fragile. Delphi's *omphalos* — the netted stone said to mark where Zeus's eagles met — is Greek and ancient. Cusco is glossed as the navel of the Inca world in Garcilaso's account, written after the conquest. Rapa Nui is Te Pito o te Henua, and a smooth stone near Ahu Te Pito Kura carries a name the page [glosses as “navel of light”]{claim=DEEP-C019}. Göbekli Tepe means “navel hill” in Turkish.

The founding pages' own claim is the crux: [these are different kinds of evidence, differing in language, date of first record and whether the ancient builders used the name]{claim=DEEP-C018}. This edition grades it provisionally supported on a prior — Greek, Spanish, Rapanui and Turkish are four languages recorded across some two and a half millennia — while noting that none of the four source histories has been retrieved. The sharpest test is the Turkish name. If [the modern Turkish name Göbekli Tepe describes the shape of the mound]{claim=DEEP-C015}, it is a descriptive toponym given long after the builders were gone and says nothing about what they believed. The page states exactly this, and adds that [the Kurdish names for the site mean “wish hill”]{claim=DEEP-C016}; but the ledger's one record on the site's names covers the Kurdish gloss, not the Turkish, and neither is sourced on the page. The Turkish claim is unresolved, and the research item that traces all four names to their first attestation is open.

What would change the picture: an early, builder-attested “navel” usage at two or more sites. What would settle it the other way: source histories showing, as the page proposes, that one name is a modern description, one a colonial gloss, and only Delphi's an ancient sacred designation in the language of the people who used it. A bodily metaphor for a centre is available in any language; an inherited usage would need more than this.

## Hands on the belly

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P07}

The page states that [arms and hands are carved on the central T-pillars of Enclosure D at Göbekli Tepe]{claim=DEEP-C023} — the shaft a body, the T a stylised head — a claim held on its anchor, the team's study of the central pillars not yet read. Urfa Man, the life-size limestone statue from Şanlıurfa of about 9000 BCE with dark inlaid eyes and no mouth, is described by the excavation team in its own post: [both hands seem to grab his penis]{claim=DEEP-C021}. The word matters. The founding pages observe that a hand across the abdomen and a hand at the groin are close in outline but different observations; the excavators' “grab” makes them different gestures too. The moai of Ahu Tongariki, carved some ten millennia later, meet their hands low on the abdomen above the belt. The Ponce monolith at Tiwanaku, the page reports, [holds its hands to the chest]{claim=DEEP-C050}, one of them around [a snuff tablet]{claim=DEEP-C051} — captions without records.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P08}

The founding pages offer convergence in its plainest form. [Carving limbs against a stone body can protect them from breakage]{claim=DEEP-C046}, so [material constraints are a plausible contributor to the hands-on-body pose]{claim=DEEP-C047} — graded provisionally supported on the prior that any carver of a monolith knows what happens to a free-standing arm. Equally, [material constraint as a contributor to the pose does not settle its symbolic meaning]{claim=DEEP-C048}: a constraint explains why hands rest against the body, not why at the abdomen rather than the groin or the chest. The deciding observation is a survey of stone figures in the same media from cultures with no possible connection: if the pose varies with the stone and the tool, constraint wins; if it clusters along a route, something else is happening.

## Serpents, and the feathered serpent

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P12}

Snakes are everywhere in the gallery: coiled around the Olmec figure at La Venta, gripped by the hero on the Jiroft object, projecting in feathered collars from the Temple of the Feathered Serpent at Teotihuacan. The page reports [a broad cosmic-serpent motif class in 37% of sampled traditions]{claim=DEEP-C025} — another high base rate, weakly supported on the same self-reported footing as the bird-men figure. The feathered serpent of Mesoamerica is a much more specific thing than “snake”, and any comparison worth making has to preserve the feathers, the head, the body's arrangement and its relation to a human figure.

The page adds the point that governs both catalogue results: [a catalogue's geographical distribution of a broad motif class cannot by itself distinguish independent invention from very old transmission]{claim=DEEP-C026}. The same map fits a serpent invented a hundred times and a serpent inherited once. Telling them apart takes dated intermediates or a model with stated assumptions — and the one set of excavators asked about intermediates, above, reports missing links.

The catalogue experiment's headline is the most consequential thing in the case and the least tested. The page reports that [the three broad motif classes — birds, serpents, sacred centres — are each widespread]{claim=DEEP-C056}, and that [their bundle does not stand out against the study's documentation-preserving comparisons]{claim=DEEP-C057}. If the second holds, finding birds, serpents and a sacred centre together in a tradition is no rarer than finding any comparable trio of common motifs — which convergence predicts and a common source does not. But the ledger contains no record supporting that finding, only the page's two qualifications of it; and the first claim is supported only indirectly, through the bird and serpent figures, with no number recorded for sacred centres at all. The bundle claim is unresolved, and its data are what this edition would most like to see.

## The people who brought the arts

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P09}

The narrative parallel is as arresting as the visual one. A figure arrives, often from the sea; teaches writing, agriculture, law or craft; changes human life; departs, sometimes promising to return. Oannes in Babylonia, Viracocha in the Andes, Quetzalcoatl in Mexico and Bochica among the Muisca recur in the comparison. The founding pages' caution is that the exact arrival, teaching and departure have to be read in each account, not supplied by a composite biography.

One figure has both a text and a dated image behind him, and the text is in the ledger. Berossus's *Babyloniaca* survives only in excerpts — here through Alexander Polyhistor as preserved by Syncellus — and its first fragment describes the creature that came out of the sea in the first year: [it had the whole body of a fish, but beneath the fish's head another, human, head, and joined to the tail feet like a man's]{claim=DEEP-C081}, and a human voice. It taught men writing, mathematics and knowledge of every kind — [how to build cities, found temples and make laws, how to fix borders and divide land, how to plant and harvest; in short, everything conducive to a settled and civilised life]{claim=DEEP-C092} — and, the fragment adds, [its form has been preserved in sculpture to this day]{claim=DEEP-C082}. Which sculpture, the text does not say. On a basalt basin from Assur the god Ea stands with streams flowing from his shoulders beside a sage wearing a fish's head and skin as a cloak; the page holds that [this fish-cloaked figure is the apkallu type the texts actually name]{claim=DEEP-C052}, a claim still on its anchor. What the ledger does hold is the translators' comparative table, which [sets Berossus's Oannes beside U-An, the first of the apkallu, in a king-and-sage list from Uruk]{claim=DEEP-C086}. So the textual half of the match — a fish body over a human head, and a name aligned by scholars with the first sage — is recorded; the iconographic half, that the cloaked figure on the basin is that type, is not. [Berossus's Oannes corresponds to the fish-cloaked apkallu]{claim=DEEP-C053} is graded weakly supported on that disclosed footing. Oannes is nonetheless the one civiliser in the comparison whose “brings the arts” episode can be read in a source older than the comparative literature that joined him to the others.

{plate:IMG-DEEP-P11}

At Tiwanaku, the staff-bearer with the rayed head in the centre of the Gate of the Sun is often called Viracocha. The page's claim is that [that identification is a modern one]{claim=DEEP-C028}. If so, the most-reproduced “image of Viracocha” is not evidence that the story existed before the Spanish wrote it down. Unresolved, for want of a record.

The one measured result in this theme is the founder's V1 lineup experiment. AI judges were shown a civiliser account and asked to pick its partner from a lineup; the page reports that [the claimed partner ranked first in 62.5% of completed lineups, against 9% for random pairs]{claim=DEEP-C027}. That is a real signal under the experiment's conditions, and the only evidence record in the ledger pointing toward a resemblance beyond base rates. The ledger holds no record of the experiment's own stated limitations. What it can say is what the retelling account predicts: a model that has read the comparative literature knows that Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are supposed to match, and a lineup of modern summaries would measure the similarity of modern summaries. That is the mechanism the retelling account proposes — [stories can become more alike than their originals through translation, borrowing and comparative writing]{claim=DEEP-C034} — and the Rapa Nui reliefs, read by their students against a story recorded two centuries after contact, show how routinely a modern comparison reaches for a late text. No test has yet been run on the original passages. The decisive experiment leads this edition's research order: rerun the lineup with human raters on unrecognisable passages from the sources — Berossus via his excerptors, the early Andean chroniclers, Sahagún, Simón — against random hero narratives, and see whether 62.5% survives.

The lost-civilisation account attaches to these figures its strongest claims: that the teachers were emissaries of a real, identifiable, technically advanced society of great age. The page's answer, adopted here on the prior that identity, date and capability are not properties of a resemblance, is that [similarity between motifs alone cannot establish a lost-civilisation account's claims about the source's identity, date and capabilities]{claim=DEEP-C035}. A resemblance can at most suggest a connection; who was connected to whom, when, and what they could do, needs evidence of a different kind, and none is in this ledger.

## What survives the water

Flood stories raise several questions at once: whether people remember local disasters, whether particular stories travelled, and whether traditions preserve much older environmental knowledge. The founder's text-coding pilot had an AI code the details of 263 flood-story summaries. The page reports that [the coded details cluster by region]{claim=DEEP-C031}, that [details associated with Genesis are unevenly distributed]{claim=DEEP-C054}, and that [generic flood motifs are widespread]{claim=DEEP-C055}.

Each of the four accounts can live with regional clustering: inheritance with regional drift, contact along routes, independent memory of local floods, retelling in regional missions. The uneven distribution of Genesis details is the more pointed finding, because it is what the retelling account predicts — and yet, as the page says, recording a story after contact does not establish that it was borrowed. None of the three claims has an evidence record; all are held on their anchors, and the pilot coded one compiler's summaries rather than a representative collection of original accounts. What would move them: the coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts, with the Genesis-associated details dated, where possible, to before or after missionary contact.

## Indus and rongorongo

The companion project compares the sign inventories of two undeciphered scripts and the illustrations used to connect them. Its governing claim is the one this case would apply everywhere: [a visual resemblance between signs of two undeciphered scripts does not establish shared sound, meaning or descent]{claim=DEEP-C036}. Sign shapes converge between scripts known to be unrelated; the ledger holds the principle on its anchor and none of the companion's results.

## When resemblance becomes evidence

Can the resemblance people see be measured at all? The founder's three image pilots tried to make AI judges rank objects by likeness. The page reports that [judges disagreed strongly with one another about the same objects]{claim=DEEP-C037}, and that [matching the kinds of objects in a lineup changed the lineup result]{claim=DEEP-C038}. The second has an evidence record and is weakly supported; the first is held on its anchor, unresolved.

The second is the more important. *Diagnosticity* is how much an observation decides between rival explanations. If a lineup that pits a pillar against a moai, a relief and a boulder ranks them one way, and a lineup of pillars against pillars ranks them another, then part of the original resemblance was an artefact of comparing unlike kinds — a finding about every side-by-side gallery, including the one that opens this article.

## Where this leaves the question

Read strictly, the ledger says this. The objects in the gallery are, on the whole, what the founder's captions say they are: the primaries confirm handle-like forms on Pillar 43 whose function their excavators decline to name, an Assyrian ritual bucket filled and sprinkled, a Halil Rud object that hung on a cord, a fish-bodied Oannes who taught the arts, and birdmen carved later onto an older moai. That is a finding about description, not about history. Nothing retrieved supplies what the shared-past accounts need — a dated intermediate, a route, or a specific composite rarer than chance — and two of the primaries take rungs away: the Rapa Nui birdmen are additions read against a nineteenth-century story, and the Göbekli excavators describe the chain to later Near Eastern imagery as full of missing links. The broad classes are reported widespread, a self-report the ledger holds weakly; the bundle comparison has no supporting record. The one positive signal, the civiliser lineup, awaits the test that would separate it from what the retelling account predicts. The navel parallel rests on four names whose source histories have not been traced, one of them very probably modern.

The verdict is *unresolved*, chosen rather than defaulted to. It means the featured hypothesis — that the resemblances record a shared past — has neither support nor refutation in the ledger: the primaries read so far describe the objects without testing the connection between them. It does not mean the evidence is balanced. Such evidence as there is leans toward base rates, convergence and retelling, and the primaries have made the strongest form of the shared-past account more expensive without touching its weakest.

What would change our mind, in either direction:

- A blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's — or one that does not.
- A securely dated Neolithic seal or image-bearing object from Upper Mesopotamia carrying a specific Pillar 43 motif — the arched forms, the bird with disc — a millennium or more after the site: the excavators' own named intermediate, checked.
- A count of specific composites (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) across the compared objects and a kind-matched control set.
- The four navel names traced to first attestation, with the builders' usage documented or shown absent.
- The bodies of the Jiroft and Hoa Hakananai'a papers read, and every later statement by the Göbekli team on the three forms, in case one commits to a container or a building.

The best argument for the shared past that this edition does not answer: the catalogue experiment's null result, by the page's own admission, tests broad classes rather than the specific images in the claim — so the strongest evidence against a common source has not actually been aimed at it; the lineup signal, whatever its limitations, is a measurement where the critics have so far offered only reasons; and every primary read so far has confirmed rather than corrected the founder's descriptions, so the parallel is at least drawn between correctly described things. All three are fair. All three point to the same place: the next steps are small, cheap and named, and this case waits on them.

researchStatus.note: The Tepe Telegrams discussion of Pillar 43 and the Vidale & Micheli abstract were retrieved and read. DEEP-E028 records the team's statement that no final decision on the meaning of the three forms is possible, deciding DEEP-C012 (well supported); DEEP-E025 records Schmidt's 'box-like objects with handle-like attachments' (DEEP-C067); DEEP-E035 records the authors' reading of the Jiroft wear as long suspension on a cord and DEEP-E038 their single-object caveat, deciding DEEP-C009 (provisionally supported at abstract level). The paper's body, Sweatman & Tsikritsis 2017 and the team's 2017 response remain unread; the full run of team statements is DEEP-R005's target and the Vidale body is a blocked source.

assessment.synthesis: The ledger now holds two kinds of record. The founder's self-published page supplies the experiments: base rates of 55% for a broad bird-person class (DEEP-E013, on DEEP-C005) and 37% for a cosmic serpent (DEEP-E016, on DEEP-C025), both qualified by the page's own notes on uneven coverage and on broad classes not being the specific images (DEEP-E018, DEEP-E019); the V1 civiliser lineup at 62.5% against 9% (DEEP-E020, DEEP-E021, on DEEP-C027); and the image-pilot finding that kind-matched controls change a lineup result (DEEP-E022, on DEEP-C038). All are weak self-reports. Seven primary or near-primary texts now decide object-level questions: the excavators describe the Pillar 43 forms as box-like with handle-like attachments (DEEP-E025, on DEEP-C067) and state that no final decision on their meaning is possible (DEEP-E028, on DEEP-C012); the Jiroft object's published abstract reads its wear as long suspension on a cord (DEEP-E035, on DEEP-C009), on a single object and 'far from being granted' (DEEP-E038); Wiggermann, via an unchecked transcription, names the banduddû as the reliefs' bucket, filled with water and sprinkled (DEEP-E055, on DEEP-C044); the Hoa Hakananai'a abstract places the bas-reliefs after the komari, which were added after the statue was made (DEEP-E068, DEEP-E069, on DEEP-C059), and reads them against the birdman myth as recorded in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (DEEP-E071, on DEEP-C080); Berossus's first fragment gives Oannes a fish body with a human head beneath (DEEP-E043, on DEEP-C081) and the teaching of cities, temples and laws (DEEP-E046, on DEEP-C092), and the translators align him with U-An, first of the apkallu (DEEP-E079, on DEEP-C086); the Urfa Man post has both hands grabbing the penis (DEEP-E081, on DEEP-C021); and a team member states there are too many missing links to be sure of any survival of the site's imagery into later periods (DEEP-E061, DEEP-E062, on DEEP-C072). None of these tests the thesis; they confirm what the objects are and, in two cases, remove a rung — the Rapa Nui birdmen are late additions read against a post-contact text, and the excavators report no established chain toward later Near Eastern imagery. The bundle null (DEEP-C057) still has no supporting record; the navel names, the Viracocha label, the flood coding and the AI judges' disagreement are anchor-only. The featured hypothesis therefore stands neither supported nor refuted, and the verdict is unresolved — chosen, because 'contradicted' would need the composite count or the blind lineup to have come out against it, and any supported grade would need a record pointing toward a shared past beyond base rates. Such evidence as exists leans toward convergence and retelling. The single record whose removal would most change the case verdict is DEEP-E020: without it nothing in the ledger points toward a resemblance beyond base rates, and the case would tilt from unresolved toward weak support for the conventional accounts.
assessment.steelman: The strongest case for a shared past that this assessment does not answer has three parts. First, the only evidence that could count against a common source — the page's report that the motif bundle does not stand out against comparison bundles — tests broad narrative classes, and the page itself concedes (DEEP-E019) that broad classes are not the specific images or place names in the claim; a composite of profile head, bent limb and rounded form, or of handle attachment, proportion and decoration, has never been counted against a control set, so the null has not been aimed at the hypothesis it is taken to undermine. Second, the V1 lineup produced a measured signal (DEEP-E020, DEEP-E021) under stated conditions, and the objections to it — recognisability, compression — are reasons, not measurements; until the blind human rerun is done, the one experiment in the ledger with a result favours the resemblance being real. Third, every primary read so far has confirmed the founder's descriptions rather than corrected them: the Göbekli forms are handle-like in the excavator's own words (DEEP-E025), the Jiroft object hung on a cord (DEEP-E035), the banduddû is a ritual bucket (DEEP-E055), Oannes is fish-bodied and teaches the arts (DEEP-E043, DEEP-E046) — so proponents can say the parallel is drawn between correctly described things, and that 'function unknown' at Göbekli Tepe is not 'function known to be other than a container'. Proponents read Berossus's remark that Oannes's form was preserved in sculpture (DEEP-E044) as tying the text to the fish-cloaked figures; the fragment does not itself say which sculpture. None of this changes a verdict, because none adds a record pointing to a connection; each names the test that would.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That a set of recurring forms and stories appear across distant ancient cultures because they descend from a shared past — one common source, or long-distance contact — rather than arising independently or being assembled after the fact by retelling and comparison. The features admitted evidence carries are: small handled objects (three box-like forms with handle-like attachments on Göbekli Tepe's Pillar 43, the Assyrian ritual bucket, a Halil Rud chlorite object worn as if hung on a cord); bird-headed figures, among them two birdmen carved onto the back of the Rapa Nui statue Hoa Hakananai'a; a teacher from the sea who brings the arts, in Berossus's Oannes; and hands held against the body of a stone figure, in Urfa Man. Held here on anchors only: sacred centres named as a navel, the feathered serpent's antiquity, and flood stories that few survive.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not in whether the outlines rhyme, nor now in what most of the objects are — the primaries confirm the descriptions — but in five places. Whether the broad classes' high base rates dispose of the parallels, or whether the specific composites are rarer than chance (no count exists). Whether the civiliser lineup signal measures the original accounts or the modern summaries that compress them. Whether any dated intermediate can be produced for any parallel, given that the excavators themselves report missing links and the Rapa Nui birdmen are additions read against a nineteenth-century text. Whether the four navel names share anything beyond a bodily metaphor, given their different languages, dates and users. And whether resemblance can be measured at all when kind-matched controls change the ranking.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: For the shared-past account: dated intermediates and a plausible route for any one parallel — most concretely, a securely dated Neolithic seal from Upper Mesopotamia carrying a specific Pillar 43 motif a millennium or more after the site; a specific composite (pose plus object plus arrangement; handle attachment plus proportion plus decoration) occurring across the compared objects more often than across a kind-matched control set from unconnected cultures; a blind human lineup of original civiliser passages that beats random pairs by a margin like V1's; an early, builder-attested navel usage at two or more sites. Against it: the catalogue's bundle comparison data released and holding under narrower classes; the blind rerun collapsing toward chance; source histories showing the Göbekli name modern and descriptive, the Cusco gloss colonial, the Viracocha identification modern; a team publication committing the three Göbekli forms to buildings rather than containers; the Hoa Hakananai'a reliefs dated in absolute terms to the post-contact period.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Broad motif classes are common everywhere — a bird-person in more than half of sampled traditions, a cosmic serpent in more than a third, by the page's own count — so meeting them in two cultures is the expectation, not the anomaly. Shared bodies, animals, materials and practical problems produce convergent forms: a handle is how anyone carries a thing, hands against a stone body are how a monolith keeps its arms. The compared set is selected for resemblance from a very large pool of objects, and comparing unlike kinds inflates the likeness that kind-matched controls remove. The compared pieces are far apart in time and, where dated, late: the Rapa Nui birdmen are additions to an older statue and are read by their students against a myth recorded after European contact, and the Göbekli excavators report no established chain from their imagery to anything later. Stories converge through translation, comparative writing and missionary contact, so compressed modern summaries of Oannes, Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are more alike than their originals. The navel names are four languages recorded across two and a half millennia, one of them a modern Turkish description of a mound's shape.

components.label: Base rates from the catalogue and coding pilots
components.note: The page reports 55% for a bird-person class (DEEP-E013, on DEEP-C005) and 37% for a cosmic serpent (DEEP-E016, on DEEP-C025), qualified by uneven coverage and the gap between broad classes and specific images (DEEP-E018, DEEP-E019). Self-reports, data not in hand. The bundle null (DEEP-C057) and the flood-coding claims (DEEP-C031, DEEP-C054) have no supporting record.

components.label: The civiliser lineup against retelling
components.note: DEEP-E020 and DEEP-E021 (on DEEP-C027) give 62.5% against 9% as the page's own report; no record carries the experiment's limitations. The retelling mechanism (DEEP-C034) is graded on a prior. Oannes's textual side is now recorded — fish body with human head (DEEP-E043, on DEEP-C081) and the teaching of the arts (DEEP-E046, on DEEP-C092) — but the blind test on original passages has not been run.

components.label: Handled objects: shape known, function separately argued
components.note: Schmidt describes box-like objects with handle-like attachments (DEEP-E025, on DEEP-C067); the team states no final decision on their meaning is possible (DEEP-E028, on DEEP-C012). The Jiroft object hung on a cord by the authors' reading (DEEP-E035, on DEEP-C009), on one object and 'far from being granted' (DEEP-E038). The banduddû is the reliefs' ritual bucket, filled and sprinkled, seen via an unchecked transcription (DEEP-E055, on DEEP-C044). The comparison is thus between a known bucket, a probable hung container and three forms of unknown function; no composite count exists.

components.label: Chronology and intermediates
components.note: Hoa Hakananai'a's reliefs succeed komari that were added after the statue was made (DEEP-E068, DEEP-E069, on DEEP-C059) and are read against the birdman myth as recorded in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries (DEEP-E071, on DEEP-C080); the abstract gives no absolute date. A Göbekli team member states there are too many missing links to be sure of any survival of the site's imagery (DEEP-E061, DEEP-E062, on DEEP-C072). What is supported is the lateness of one leg and the absence of an established chain; this raises the cost of a common source without establishing convergence.

components.label: The navel names
components.note: The four names' source histories are unretrieved. DEEP-C018 is graded on the prior that Greek, Spanish, Rapanui and Turkish records span two and a half millennia; the Turkish descriptive gloss (DEEP-C015) is anchor-only, the one record on the site's names (DEEP-E024, on DEEP-C016) covering only the Kurdish 'wish hill'.

components.label: Whether resemblance can be measured, and by what rules
components.note: Kind-matched controls change a lineup result (DEEP-E022, on DEEP-C038); the judges' disagreement (DEEP-C037) is anchor-only. The method claims (DEEP-C002, DEEP-C004, DEEP-C026, DEEP-C035, DEEP-C047, DEEP-C065) are graded on priors stated as priors. The excavators' 'grab' for Urfa Man's gesture (DEEP-E081, on DEEP-C021) shows how a primary description sharpens a distinction — groin versus abdomen — that a side-by-side gallery blurs.

researchPriority.reason: The decisive tests are desk-level and cheap — a blind human lineup on original passages, a check of the excavators' named intermediate in Atakuman's seal corpus, four source histories — and each would move several verdicts. But none tests the strong shared-past thesis directly, the primaries read so far have described objects rather than connections, and the domain has been argued for a century without a design that separates transmission from convergence; the return on the small named steps is real, the return on the grand question uncertain.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record. Graded on a disclosed prior: it is the working rule of comparative iconography that a resemblance underdetermines its history without dates, contexts and connections. The ledger's own records illustrate the rule — DEEP-E028, attached to DEEP-C012, shows the excavators refusing to assign a function to Pillar 43's forms from their shape alone — but that record carries DEEP-C012, not this claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: Two things looking alike tells you nothing about history until you know when and where each was made, how they differ, and whether their makers could have met.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A rule of method, not an observation; it decides nothing between the four accounts but sets the standard every parallel in the case must meet.
treatment.strongestObjection: Taken strictly, a rule that no resemblance counts without full contextual data can make any diffusion hypothesis untestable in practice, since the data are rarely complete.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A documented case in which resemblance alone, without dates or contexts, predicted a connection later confirmed by independent evidence.
A formal model in which resemblance has measurable evidential weight independent of context.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The ledger holds only two qualifying records for this claim (DEEP-E018, DEEP-E019), which limit the catalogue's coverage and the reach of broad classes; no record supports the positive finding that the bundle does not stand out. The finding is held on the page's anchor, its data and comparison method not in hand.

treatment.plainLanguage: The founder's own experiment reportedly found that birds, serpents and sacred centres occur together no more often than any other trio of common motifs would.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If it held under narrow classes it would be the strongest single result for convergence and against a common source; as it stands it tests broad classes the page admits are not the claim's specifics.
treatment.strongestObjection: The comparison bundles and the documentation-preserving procedure are unpublished; without them the null cannot be distinguished from a test too coarse to detect anything.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data and comparison bundles released and the null reproduced under narrower motif definitions — or failing to reproduce.
A count of specific composites against kind-matched controls, which would supersede the broad-class result in either direction.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E020 and DEEP-E021 record the page's own statement of the 62.5% and 9% figures; both are weak self-reports with run data not retrieved, and 'completed lineups' implies incomplete runs the page does not enumerate. No record carries the experiment's stated limitations.

treatment.plainLanguage: When AI judges were shown a civiliser story and a lineup, they picked the claimed matching figure first far more often than chance.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The only record pointing to resemblance beyond base rates, but it cannot distinguish similarity of the original accounts from similarity of recognisable modern summaries — exactly what the retelling account predicts.
treatment.strongestObjection: A model that has read the comparative literature knows Viracocha and Quetzalcoatl are supposed to match; the lineup may measure the literature, not the myths.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind human lineup on unrecognisable source-level passages that reproduces a margin like V1's — or collapses toward chance.
Release of the run data showing the completed and incomplete lineups and the prompts used.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: convergence of detail between an original and its retelling is a documented phenomenon in the history of comparative mythology, and the mechanism needs no exotic assumption. No evidence record in the ledger documents a specific convergence for the civiliser figures.

treatment.plainLanguage: Stories from different places can end up sounding more alike than they originally were, once they have been translated, borrowed and written about together.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It is the mechanism of the retelling account and the leading explanation of the lineup signal; if documented for these figures it would neutralise DEEP-C027, if refuted the signal would gain weight.
treatment.strongestObjection: A general possibility is not a demonstration; the account owes a documented case in which Oannes, Viracocha or Quetzalcoatl grew more alike between an early and a later telling.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A source audit showing the specific details shared in modern summaries are absent from the earliest attested versions.
Conversely, the earliest versions sharing the same sea arrival, teaching and departure sequence independently of one another.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: identity, date and capability of a source are not properties a resemblance can carry; they require independent evidence. No admitted record bears on it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Even if two images are connected, their likeness cannot tell you who the source was, how old, or what it could do.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Does not choose among the four accounts; it constrains the strongest variant of the common-source account, whose extra claims need a different kind of evidence.
treatment.strongestObjection: Proponents may say the extra claims are inferences from the antiquity and distribution of the parallels, not from resemblance alone — but those inferences are what the rule says need their own support.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent archaeological evidence — a site, a technology, a dated route — for the proposed source.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: a present-day distribution of a broad motif class is compatible with many histories, and separating them requires dated intermediates or an explicit model. DEEP-E061 (attached to DEEP-C072) records the excavators' view that intermediates for their site are missing, which illustrates the point without carrying this claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: A map of where a motif occurs cannot tell you whether it was invented many times or inherited once.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A limit on what the catalogue results can show; it protects the shared-past account from the base-rate argument as much as it protects convergence from the distribution argument.
treatment.strongestObjection: Phylogeographic methods claim to separate inheritance from invention from distributions alone under stated models; the claim as worded concedes this with 'under stated models'.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A validated model, tested on motifs of known history, that recovers transmission versus invention from distribution alone.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Only qualifying records are attached (DEEP-E018, DEEP-E019). The claim leans, as disclosed, on sibling records: DEEP-E013 (on DEEP-C005) reports the bird class at 55% and DEEP-E016 (on DEEP-C025) the serpent class at 37%; no record gives a figure for sacred centres. Two of three classes evidenced weakly, one not at all.

treatment.plainLanguage: Birds, serpents and sacred centres each turn up in a large share of the world's recorded traditions.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: High base rates make a bird or serpent in two cultures expected; the claim underwrites the convergence account's first prediction but says nothing about the specific images.
treatment.strongestObjection: The catalogue's coverage is uneven precisely for the regions compared, and the sacred-centre figure is nowhere recorded.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The sacred-centre frequency recorded from the coded data.
Recoding with narrower classes showing the specific images are rare.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E013 and DEEP-E014 record the page's statement of the 55% figure; DEEP-E015, DEEP-E018 and DEEP-E019 qualify its reach. All weak self-reports; the coded data and the underlying catalogue are not in hand.

treatment.plainLanguage: In the founder's sample of 926 traditions, more than half include some kind of bird-person.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes a baseline that disarms the weakest form of the bird-man parallel; it does not address the composite of head, limb and rounded form.
treatment.strongestObjection: The class is broad enough to include winged souls and feathered dancers, and the sample under-covers the ancient Near East and Rapa Nui.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data released and the proportion reproduced by an independent coder.
A frequency for the specific composite rather than the class.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E016 records the page's 37% figure; DEEP-E017, DEEP-E018 and DEEP-E019 qualify it. Weak self-report, data not retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: In the founder's sample, more than a third of traditions have a cosmic serpent of some kind.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A high base rate for 'snake' that leaves the feathered serpent — a specific composite — uncounted.
treatment.strongestObjection: The catalogue category describes a selected class and dataset; it says nothing about the feathered serpent's specificity.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent reproduction of the coded proportion.
A count of feathered or plumed serpents specifically across the sample.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: bird-headed deity, feathered costume and human-to-bird transformation are distinct concepts in the anthropological literature. No admitted record sorts the gallery's images among them.

treatment.plainLanguage: 'Bird-man' covers three different ideas — a god with a bird's head, a person dressed in feathers, and a person turning into a bird.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the compared images fall into different categories the single parallel becomes three weaker ones; a rung under the bird-men theme.
treatment.strongestObjection: Proponents may say the categories blur in practice — a masked dancer represents a transformation — so the distinction does not weaken the parallel.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A coded sorting of the gallery images by category, showing most compared pairs share one.
Iconographic evidence that the Göbekli vulture, the Nimrud genie and the Rapa Nui birdman belong to the same category.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E068 and DEEP-E069 record the published abstract's sequence: statue made with a tapering base, two komari subsequently added, bas-relief carvings succeeding them. Moderate strength, abstract only, relative sequence with no absolute date.

treatment.plainLanguage: The birdmen on the back of Hoa Hakananai'a were carved onto a statue that already existed.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Places the Rapa Nui leg of the bird-man parallel later than the monument it decorates and, with DEEP-C080, ties it to a post-contact recorded myth; costly for a common source, neutral between contact and convergence.
treatment.strongestObjection: Relative sequence is not date; the reliefs could still be pre-contact by centuries.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An absolute date for the reliefs from the paper's body or the museum record.
Evidence that the birdman motif on Rapa Nui predates the statue elsewhere on the island.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior and a disclosed sibling basis: DEEP-E028 (on DEEP-C012) shows the excavators know the shape of the Göbekli forms and decline their function, and DEEP-E035 (on DEEP-C009) shows the Jiroft object's function argued from wear rather than outline — the separation in practice.

treatment.plainLanguage: Knowing what an object looks like is a different question from knowing what it was for.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A rule that governs the handled-object theme; it decides nothing itself but makes the comparison of a known bucket with unknown forms visible as such.
treatment.strongestObjection: Form follows function often enough that a shared shape is some evidence of shared use.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A team publication identifying the Göbekli forms as containers, which would collapse the separation for this case.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E055 records, via a blog transcription of Wiggermann 1992, that the banduddû was filled with water in rituals and used to sprinkle over the man. Weak: secondhand, transcription unchecked against the printed page, and the cone half of the 'purifier' reading is not in the transcribed text.

treatment.plainLanguage: Assyrian ritual texts describe the genie's bucket being filled with water and used to sprinkle.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Makes the Nimrud object a known ritual vessel, so the parallel sets a known bucket beside forms of unknown function; it neither helps nor hurts a common source until the Göbekli forms are identified.
treatment.strongestObjection: The record is a transcription on a personal blog with visibly garbled transliterations; the printed page has not been read.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Wiggermann 1992, p. 66 read and the transcription confirmed or corrected.
A ritual text naming the cone and its use alongside the bucket.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E028 is a strong record of the excavation team's own statement that a final decision on the meaning of the three forms is not possible. DEEP-E025 (on DEEP-C067) shows the excavator's first description used 'box-like' and 'handle-like' without a function, a disclosed sibling basis. Confidence moderate because the statement is a 2016 blog post by a team member and later team publications are unchecked.

treatment.plainLanguage: The people who excavated Pillar 43 say they cannot tell what the three handled shapes represent.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Removes the Göbekli leg of the 'handbag' parallel from the class of known containers; the comparison becomes one of shapes only, which convergence explains as easily as descent.
treatment.strongestObjection: 'Uncertain' is not 'not a container'; the team's alternative reading (buildings in section) is offered as a possibility, not a finding.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A later team publication committing to a container or a building.
Wear or residue evidence on the pillar's relief, which is not expected.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E035 records the published abstract's reading of the strong handle wear as long suspension on a cord; DEEP-E034 records the wear as visible on handle and contour; DEEP-E038 records the authors' own limit that the inference rests on a single object and is far from granted. The claim's truth condition — that the study reports handle wear of that kind — is met at abstract level; the object's identity with the photographed piece is unconfirmed.

treatment.plainLanguage: A specialist study reads the wear on one Jiroft 'handbag' as showing it hung from a cord for a long time.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes that one Halil Rud object was a hung container; this is compatible with every account and says nothing about the other three objects.
treatment.strongestObjection: One object, hedged by its own authors; the class of 'intercultural style' handled objects includes readings as weights.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The paper's body read, with the wear photographs and the iron-repair discussion.
Wear analysis of further specimens.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E061 and DEEP-E062 record a team member's reply that there are too many missing links to be sure of the extent of any survival of Early Neolithic imagery or of changes in its meaning. The claim's truth condition — a team member's published statement — is met; the records are weak because the statement is an informal comment-thread reply.

treatment.plainLanguage: The Göbekli Tepe excavators say there is no established chain linking their imagery to later Near Eastern objects.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The contact account requires dated intermediates; the people best placed to produce them report their absence while naming one candidate class (later seals). A positive check would give the contact account its first local intermediate; a negative one closes the named route.
treatment.strongestObjection: Absence of established links in 2016 is a statement about the state of research, not about the past; the same reply cites evidence that some imagery survives into seals.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Atakuman 2015 read and a securely dated seal carrying a specific Pillar 43 motif recorded.
A later team publication asserting continuity into a named class of objects.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: the four names are in Greek, Spanish, Rapanui and Turkish, first recorded across roughly two and a half millennia, and only the Greek is plausibly a name used by the sanctuary's own users. None of the four source histories has been retrieved.

treatment.plainLanguage: The four 'navel' names are not the same kind of evidence: they differ in language, in when they were first written down, and in whether the builders themselves used them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If true the navel parallel reduces to a shared bodily metaphor; if any two names share an early, builder-attested usage the parallel would be the most specific in the case.
treatment.strongestObjection: Different recording dates do not prove different origins; a modern Turkish name could preserve an older local tradition.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The earliest attestation of each name's 'navel' meaning traced in primary texts.
A pre-modern or indigenous attestation of the navel meaning at Cusco or Rapa Nui independent of colonial glossing.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record. The one record on the site's names (DEEP-E024, attached to DEEP-C016) covers the Kurdish gloss 'wish hill', not the Turkish name's descriptive origin.

treatment.plainLanguage: 'Göbekli Tepe' is a modern Turkish name that just describes the mound's rounded shape.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If the name is a modern description, the site's place in the navel parallel disappears; it is the cheapest of the four source histories to settle.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unsourced on the page; a local sacred-place tradition attached to the hill has been asserted elsewhere and is unexamined here.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A Turkish toponymic or excavation-report source giving the name's origin.
Documentation of a pre-modern sacred designation of the hill in any local language.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Anchor-only. Graded on a disclosed prior: free-standing limbs in stone break, and carvers of monoliths routinely keep arms against the body. No admitted record tests the pose against media or cultures.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvers may fold a stone figure's hands onto its body partly because arms that stick out snap off.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The convergence account's mechanism for the hands theme; it explains hands-on-body but not the placement, so it disarms the general parallel and leaves the specific one open.
treatment.strongestObjection: Constraint does not explain why hands rest on the abdomen rather than the chest or groin — and the ledger's one primary on Urfa Man (DEEP-E081, on DEEP-C021) shows a grasping gesture the constraint does not require.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A survey of stone figures in comparable media from unconnected cultures showing the pose varies with material rather than region.
Clustering of the abdominal placement along a plausible route.

claimAssessments.reasoning: The records attached to this claim (DEEP-E075, DEEP-E076) are context only. The grade rests on a disclosed sibling basis: DEEP-E043 (on DEEP-C081) records Berossus's Oannes as fish-bodied with a human head beneath, and DEEP-E079 (on DEEP-C086) records the translators' alignment of Oannes with U-An, first of the apkallu. The iconographic half — that the fish-cloaked figure is the apkallu type the texts name (DEEP-C052) — is anchor-only, so the correspondence is inferred, not stated by any record.

treatment.plainLanguage: The fish-bodied sage Berossus calls Oannes is the same kind of figure as the fish-cloaked sages carved beside the god Ea.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Gives one civiliser a documented text and a candidate image within a single culture; it establishes that Oannes's episode is old, not that it is connected to any other civiliser.
treatment.strongestObjection: Berossus says the form was preserved in sculpture but not which; the match to the fish-cloaked type is a scholarly inference the ledger has not yet recorded from an Assyriological source.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An Assyriological source identifying the fish-cloaked figures as apkallu by name.
The apkallu texts read and found to describe a different dress.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record; no Andean chronicle or art-historical source has been read for the identification's history.

treatment.plainLanguage: Calling the Gate of the Sun's central figure 'Viracocha' is a modern label, not something the Tiwanaku people or early chroniclers said.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If modern, the most-reproduced image of the Andean civiliser is no evidence that the story predates the Spanish; a rung under the civiliser theme and the retelling account.
treatment.strongestObjection: A modern label on an image does not bear on whether the Viracocha narrative itself is pre-Hispanic, which the chroniclers' sources may show.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The earliest attribution of the Gate of the Sun figure to Viracocha traced in the literature.
A pre-modern source naming the figure.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record; the pilot's coded data and its clustering measure are not in hand.

treatment.plainLanguage: In the founder's coding of 263 flood-story summaries, stories from the same region shared details.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Regional clustering is compatible with all four accounts; the finding, if it held, would not choose among them.
treatment.strongestObjection: One AI coded one compiler's summaries; the clustering could be the compiler's.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The coded data released and re-coded by human readers against original texts.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record.

treatment.plainLanguage: Details that echo the Genesis flood turn up in some regions' stories and not others.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Uneven distribution of a famous version's details is what the retelling account predicts; but recording after contact does not establish borrowing, and the finding is unrecorded.
treatment.strongestObjection: Unevenness could reflect the compiler's selection or missionary-era recording rather than borrowing.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The Genesis-associated details dated, where possible, to before or after missionary contact in each region.

claimAssessments.reasoning: DEEP-E022 records the page's statement that matching the kinds of objects changed the lineup result; a weak self-report with pilot data not retrieved and incomplete runs acknowledged.

treatment.plainLanguage: When the lineup compared like with like — pillars with pillars — the objects that seemed most alike changed.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If it holds, part of every side-by-side gallery's resemblance is an artefact of comparing unlike kinds — a finding about the method that produced the case's opening impression.
treatment.strongestObjection: The pilots used AI judges not shown to reproduce human resemblance judgments, with cropping and repeated objects constraining the runs.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The pilot rankings released under matched and unmatched conditions.
A human-rater replication with kind-matched controls.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor with no admitted evidence record; no inter-judge agreement statistic is in the ledger.

treatment.plainLanguage: Different AI judges looking at the same pair of objects often disagreed about how alike they were.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If measured low, agreement would show the resemblance people see is not stably measurable by these tools; it bears on method, not on the objects.
treatment.strongestObjection: Disagreement among AI judges says nothing about agreement among human viewers, whose judgment the case actually concerns.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The pilots' agreement statistics released.
A human inter-rater study on the same pairs.
